title: Closures
summary: How functions remember the variables around them: private state, loops and function factories.

misconceptions.description: Believes a function keeps a copy of the value a variable had when the function was written, so later changes are not seen.
Believes a function can use only its own parameters and variables, not those declared outside it.
Believes the variables of a function are deleted when it returns, so a function created inside can no longer read them.
Believes every call of a factory function shares one set of variables.
Believes a captured variable starts again from its first value each time the inner function is called.
Believes a variable kept in a closure can be read as a property of the returned object.
Takes the wrong run of a line that executes many times, counting one run too few or too many.
Believes a var in a for loop gets a fresh variable for each pass, so each function keeps its own value.
Believes the loop variable keeps the last value the loop body saw, not the value that ended the loop.
Believes a let in a for loop is shared by all passes, as var is.
Believes var and let give the same result when functions are created in a loop.
Believes the function returned by a factory uses only its own argument and not the one given to the outer call.

conceptCard.title: Functions keep their surroundings
conceptCard.body: A function can use variables from the place where it was written, even after that place has finished running. It keeps a link to the variable itself, not a copy of its value. If the variable changes later, the function sees the new value.

conceptCard.title: State that nobody else can reach
conceptCard.body: A variable inside a function cannot be reached from outside. If the function returns other functions that use it, only those functions can read or change it. Each call of the outer function makes a new, separate variable.

conceptCard.title: One variable or one per pass
conceptCard.body: A closure keeps the variable, not one value. A var loop has a single variable for the whole loop, so every function made in it sees its final value. A let loop makes a new variable for each pass, so each function keeps its own.

conceptCard.title: Functions that make functions
conceptCard.body: A function that returns a function is a factory: it remembers the argument it received. Calling f(a)(b) means calling f with a, then calling the result with b. Splitting arguments this way is called currying.

items.prompt: Which statement is true about this code?

options.text: back can still read sign after marker has finished.
options.feedback: Right. The returned function keeps access to sign, so back() prints "to Elm".

options.text: sign is removed when marker returns, so back() prints undefined.
options.feedback: A variable stays alive as long as a function that uses it exists. back keeps sign available.

options.text: Every call of marker shares one sign, so back would show the latest call's sign.
options.feedback: Each call of marker creates its own sign. Here marker runs once, and a later call would not change back.

items.explanation: A function remembers the variables around the place where it was written. back was written inside marker, so it keeps sign even though marker has already returned.
hints: Compare when marker runs with when back runs.
A function written inside another keeps the outer variables it uses.
Ask whether sign is still reachable by back after line 5.

items.prompt: A hit counter returns 1 on its second call instead of 2. Tap the line that stops it counting, then pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. The result is stored back in hits, so the second call sees 1 and returns 2.
The parameter hides the private hits. visit() passes nothing, so hits is undefined and the result is NaN.
The braces make a body with no return, so the call gives undefined, and hits is still never changed.

hints: Look at what line 3 does with the result of hits + 1.
